lesson.title: Organizing the Pulpits: The Southern Christian Leadership Conference
lesson.summary: Founded in 1957 by Martin Luther King Jr. and other Black ministers in the wake of the Montgomery Bus Boycott, the Southern Christian Leadership Conference built a regional network of churches to organize nonviolent protest across the South.
lesson.body:
The Montgomery Bus Boycott proved that a local Black community, organized around its churches and led with discipline, could force real change against a segregated system. Martin Luther King Jr. and other ministers who had helped lead the boycott believed that model needed to be extended beyond Montgomery, since segregation was not a Montgomery problem but a regional and national one. In 1957, King joined with fellow ministers, including Ralph Abernathy of Montgomery, Fred Shuttlesworth of Birmingham, C. K. Steele of Tallahassee, and Joseph Lowery, to found a new organization in Atlanta, Georgia, called the Southern Christian Leadership Conference, with King elected as its first president.

SCLC's strategy grew directly out of the Montgomery experience and the Black church tradition most of its founders came from. Rather than organizing through a mass individual membership the way older organizations like the NAACP did, SCLC worked by affiliating with and mobilizing existing Black churches across the South, using their networks, meeting spaces, and moral authority to organize nonviolent protest campaigns. The strategy reflected King's own theology, blending the Christian idea of redemptive suffering with the disciplined nonviolent resistance associated with Mohandas Gandhi's independence movement in India.

This church centered, minister led approach gave SCLC real strengths: an existing infrastructure of buildings and trusted local leaders across many Southern cities, and a moral vocabulary, drawn from scripture and sermon, that resonated powerfully with its target audience and with the broader American public watching from a distance. It would also, within a few years, stand in contrast to a very different kind of organization built by younger activists who wanted a more grassroots, less hierarchical structure. That organization, the Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee, would work alongside SCLC through the early 1960s even as the two groups sometimes disagreed sharply about strategy and pace, a tension that shaped much of the civil rights movement's internal history during this period.
